title: Drifting like an infant
hook: others are busy and bright; I alone drift, like a baby not yet smiling (Tao Te Ching 20)

segments.voice: Yesterday, chapter nineteen: plain silk and uncarved wood, and your line was uncarved. Did you use something plain, and let it stay plain? Today the book speaks in the first person. Day one thousand eighty-two.

The square is full. Music, lanterns, food going around on platters, people calling to each other across the crowd. Everyone has somewhere to be and something to say. Off to one side, a single person stands still. Not sulking, not judging. Just not swept up. If someone asked what they were doing, the honest answer would be nothing much. Chapter twenty of the Tao Te Ching is spoken by that person. It says I, and the I sounds a little lonely, and a little free.
screen: `A FULL SQUARE.` → `ONE PERSON STANDS STILL.` → `CHAPTER TWENTY SAYS I.`

segments.voice: First, the crowd at the feast. The chapter describes the people around the speaker as bright and pleased, as if they were at a great banquet, or climbing a terrace in spring. Nothing in the text says they are wicked. They are simply full, busy, sure of what they're doing. Second, I alone, adrift. Against that brightness the speaker sets himself. Others have more than enough; he seems to have lost something. Others are sharp and clear; he seems dull and murky. He is restless as the sea, blown about like a wind with nowhere to stop. It reads like a confession of failure, and some readers think it's meant to sound that way, a little wry, a little sad. Third, an infant not yet smiling. Then comes the picture at the center. In Legge's translation: "I am like an infant which has not yet smiled." A newborn hasn't started performing yet. It hasn't learned to smile on cue, to look interested, to keep up. It just drifts in the room, taking everything in. The speaker has stayed, or gone back, to that early place, before the social face is put on. Fourth, fed by the mother. The chapter ends by naming what makes the speaker different from everyone else: he values being fed by the mother. Some readers take the mother to be the Tao itself, the source this book keeps returning to. So the drifting isn't aimless after all. It is a person who stopped grabbing at the banquet because they are already being fed.
screen: `THE CROWD AT THE FEAST.` · `I ALONE, ADRIFT.` · `AN INFANT NOT YET SMILING.` · `FED BY THE MOTHER.` · then, large: `I AM LIKE AN INFANT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be unbusy. For the next two minutes, don't meditate and don't improve anything. Let your face go slack, the way a face looks before anyone is watching. Let your eyes rest on whatever is in front of them without naming it. If a task tugs at you, let it tug, and stay where you are. You're the one standing still at the edge of the square. Later today, if you can, give yourself ten minutes like this. The bell holds the time.
Drifting like an infant. Chapter twenty's picture of someone not swept up by the crowd, unperformed, still being fed by the source. Today's word.
Your line: drifting. When you catch yourself performing today, the ready smile, the busy look, the keeping up, let your face rest for one breath. Day one thousand eighty-two.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter twenty as permission to do nothing for a while: a stretch of unscheduled time, with no goal, when they are not trying to keep up with anyone.

original.note: Chinese, yīng'ér zhī wèi hái: an infant not yet smiling, from Tao Te Ching 20.

trapdoor: what you thought: drifting like an infant means being lazy or lost.
what it means: not swept up by the crowd, not performing, like a newborn before it has learned to smile on cue.
what a scholar hears: chapter twenty is spoken in the first person, and it ends with the speaker valuing being fed by the mother, read as the Tao.

notes: Verify the Legge 1891 wording: 'I am like an infant which has not yet smiled.'

Paraphrased from chapter 20: the crowd 'as if enjoying a full banquet, as if mounted on a tower in spring'; the speaker dull, murky, restless as the sea, blown with nowhere to stop; the closing line about valuing the nursing mother. Confirm the paraphrase.
'The book usually talks about the sage' and 'here it says I' is a general reading of the text's voice; other chapters also use 'I'. Check the framing is fair.
'Some readers take the mother to be the Tao' is interpretation (Legge glosses it so); confirm.
Day 1072 already used the infant image (chapter 10). This day takes the angle of the unperformed self apart from the crowd instead; check for overlap.
Day 1081 was not on disk when this was drafted; the review follows its index (pu, uncarved).
Original 嬰兒之未孩: some editions read 如嬰兒之未孩; pronunciation guide is approximate.
